usage: the thing liked takes the object marker 을/를, not 이/가
도 'also' replaces 은/는 here; never say 저도는
정말 or 진짜 in front turns up the warmth
별로 + negative is the gentle way to refuse a preference
examples: 저는 한국 음식을 좋아해요.
I like Korean food.
the bare polite present states a steady, ongoing preference
우리 강아지가 산책을 정말 좋아해요.
Our puppy really loves walks.
third-person liker takes 이/가 (강아지가), the liked thing still takes 을/를
저는 매운 음식은 별로 안 좋아해요.
I don't really like spicy food.
real refusal: 은 marks the contrast topic, 별로...안 softens the no
nuance: 좋아하다 is an action verb meaning 'to like / be fond of', so it describes a person actively having a preference and takes the object marker 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요. Contrast it with the adjective 좋다 ('to be good/nice'), which describes the thing itself and takes 이/가: 커피가 좋아요 ('coffee is nice / I feel good about coffee'). The dividing line is who is in the spotlight — 좋아하다 puts the liker on stage, 좋다 puts the liked thing on stage. Be careful with 사랑하다 ('to love'): Koreans reserve it for deep romantic or familial love and rarely say it about food or hobbies, where English happily uses 'love' — so 'I love coffee' is 커피를 좋아해요, not 커피를 사랑해요. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly: 하다 → 해요, giving 좋아해요 / 좋아합니다 / 좋아했어요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is copying English subject logic and saying 커피가 좋아해요 with 이/가; once it is a 좋아하다 sentence, the food must take 을/를.

mistakes: Saying 커피가 좋아해요 with the subject marker — because the verb 좋아하다 needs an object, the food must take 을/를: 커피를 좋아해요.
Using 사랑하다 for liking food or pastimes (커피를 사랑해요) — 사랑하다 sounds like deep romantic/familial love in Korean; for everyday fondness use 좋아하다.
Confusing it with the adjective 좋다 and saying 저는 커피를 좋아요 — if you use the object 를 you must use the verb 좋아해요, not 좋아요.

usage: the disliked thing takes the object marker 을/를
안 + 싫어해요 is a mild 'it's fine with me'
정말/진짜 makes it strong and blunt — use with care
the polite escape hatch: prefer this over a blunt 싫어해요
examples: 저는 추운 날씨를 싫어해요.
I dislike cold weather.
object 를 on the disliked thing; plain steady aversion
제 동생은 야채를 싫어해요.
My younger sibling dislikes vegetables.
third-person disliker takes 은/는 or 이/가, the food keeps 을/를
그 영화는 별로 안 좋아해요.
I don't really like that movie.
polite real-life softening — Koreans dodge 싫어해요 in front of others
nuance: 싫어하다 is the action verb 'to dislike / hate' and, like its opposite 좋아하다, takes the object marker 을/를: 벌레를 싫어해요. Its adjective partner is 싫다 ('to be unpleasant / not want to'), which takes 이/가 and points at the thing or the feeling itself: 벌레가 싫어요. The verb describes a person's standing dislike, while 싫다 often voices an in-the-moment 'ugh, I don't want to'. The near-synonym to watch is 미워하다, which is 'to resent/hate a person' with an emotional, almost grudge-like color — you 미워하다 someone who hurt you, but you 싫어하다 cold weather or homework. Register matters most here: 싫어해요 is socially strong, so saying 그 사람을 싫어해요 to someone's face is quite blunt; Koreans habitually soften with 별로 ('not really') or simply switch to 별로 안 좋아해요. As a 하다 verb it is regular: 하다 → 해요 (싫어해요 / 싫어합니다 / 싫어했어요). Pitfall: marking the object with 이/가 (벌레가 싫어해요) by mirroring English — keep 을/를 with the verb.

Using 싫어해요 bluntly about a present person (그 사람을 싫어해요) in front of others — it sounds harsh; soften to 별로 안 좋아해요 or 별로예요.
Reaching for 미워하다 for things like weather or food — 미워하다 is resentment aimed at a person; for objects and situations use 싫어하다.

usage: past 알았어요 often means 'I came to know / realized'
잘 'well' is the natural intensifier with 알다
알겠어요 acknowledges new info; 알아요 claims you already knew
examples: 저는 그 식당을 잘 알아요.
I know that restaurant well.
잘 알아요 = solid familiarity; object 를 on 식당
이 단어 뜻을 알아요?
Do you know what this word means?
rising-intonation question; 뜻을 알다 'know the meaning'
아, 이제 알겠어요. 가르쳐 줘서 고마워요.
Ah, I get it now. Thanks for explaining.
real moment of understanding uses 알겠어요, not 알아요
nuance: 알다 means 'to know / be aware of / be acquainted with' and takes the object marker 을/를: 저 사람을 알아요. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb: the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific ㅅ, giving 압니다 (not 알습니다) and 아세요 (not 알으세요), but the ㄹ stays before vowel endings, so the everyday polite form is 알아요. Two contrasts are essential. First, its opposite is not the negative 안 알아요 — that is wrong — but the separate verb 모르다, so 'I don't know' is 몰라요. Second, 알다 vs 알겠다: 알아요 claims knowledge you already hold ('I know that'), while 알겠어요 signals you have just understood or accepted something ('I see / got it / will do'), which is why a polite 'understood' is 알겠습니다, never 압니다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: forming 'don't know' as 안 알아요 instead of 몰라요, and keeping the ㄹ to say 알습니다 instead of 압니다.

usage: the thing not known takes 을/를, like 알다
잘 몰라요 softens an outright 'I don't know'
겠 adds tentative politeness — the most natural soft 'no idea'
There's a lot I don't know
모르는 + noun is the relative-clause form 'things (I) don't know'
examples: 죄송해요, 저는 길을 잘 몰라요.
Sorry, I don't really know the way.
polite apology + 잘 몰라요 to be gentle
그 사람 이름을 몰랐어요.
I didn't know that person's name.
past 몰랐어요 from the 르-irregular stem
글쎄요, 저도 잘 모르겠어요. 같이 찾아볼까요?
Hmm, I'm not sure either. Shall we look it up together?
real fumble: 모르겠어요 sounds far softer than a flat 몰라요
nuance: 모르다 is the standalone verb 'to not know / be unaware of', the lexical opposite of 알다, and it likewise takes the object marker 을/를: 길을 몰라요. It is a 르-irregular: when an 아/어 ending attaches, the 르 stem doubles the ㄹ and the vowel drops, so 모르 + 아요 → 몰라요 (never 모르아요) and the past is 몰랐어요. The crucial register tool is 겠: 잘 모르겠어요 ('I'm not quite sure') is markedly softer and more natural than a blunt 몰라요, which can sound curt or even dismissive depending on tone, so Koreans lean on the 겠 form constantly when admitting ignorance politely. Compare 모르다 with 헷갈리다 ('to be confused / mix things up'): 모르다 is having no information at all, while 헷갈리다 is having information but getting it tangled. The English-speaker pitfall is the conjugation — applying a regular pattern to get 모르아요 instead of the irregular 몰라요 — and forgetting that the smooth, courteous version is 잘 모르겠어요.

Blurting a bare 몰라요 when asked something — it can sound curt; soften with 잘 모르겠어요 to stay polite.
Using 모르다 when you mean you mixed two things up — that is 헷갈리다 (e.g. 이름이 헷갈려요 'I keep confusing the names'), not 몰라요.

usage: the place of residence takes 에 (static location), not 에서
혼자 'alone' sits right before the verb
I want to live in Korea
with 살다 about an active life-experience, 에서 is also used
examples: 저는 지금 서울에 살아요.
I live in Seoul now.
residence with 에; 지금 'now' marks current address
부모님은 부산에 사세요.
My parents live in Busan.
honorific 사세요 for elders — note the ㄹ has dropped
저는 언젠가 제주도에서 살고 싶어요.
Someday I want to live on Jeju.
future hope; 에서 + 살다 frames it as a life to be lived there
nuance: 살다 means 'to live' in two senses — to reside somewhere and to be alive — and is a ㄹ-irregular verb. The stem ㄹ disappears before ㅂ, ㄴ, and the honorific 시, producing 삽니다 (not 살읍니다), 사세요 (not 살으세요), and 사니까; before vowel endings the ㄹ stays, so the polite present is 살아요. For where you live, the default particle is the static-location 에: 서울에 살아요. Interestingly, because living is an activity carried out over time, the dynamic-location 에서 is also acceptable and common, especially with hopes and experiences (한국에서 살고 싶어요) — this is one of the few cases where both 에 and 에서 work with the same verb. Contrast 살다 with 거주하다 (居住하다, Sino-Korean 'to reside'), a stiff, formal/written word used on official forms (거주지 'place of residence'); in speech you always say 살다. The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄹ to say 살읍니다 instead of 삽니다, and reflexively choosing 에서 for every location when plain residence prefers 에.

usage: the thing created takes the object marker 을/를
ㄹ stays before 까요 — 만들까요, not 만ㄹ까요
직접 'in person/by oneself' is a common partner of 만들다
만들어 + 주세요 asks someone to make it on your behalf
examples: 저는 주말에 빵을 만들어요.
I make bread on weekends.
vowel ending keeps the ㄹ: 만들어요
엄마가 김치를 직접 만드세요.
Mom makes kimchi herself.
honorific 만드세요 — ㄹ drops before 시
우리 같이 케이크를 만들까요?
Shall we make a cake together?
invitation; ㄹ survives before 까요
nuance: 만들다 means 'to make / create / build' something concrete or abstract (food, objects, plans, rules) and takes the object marker 을/를: 음식을 만들어요. It is a ㄹ-irregular verb, so the stem ㄹ drops before ㅂ, ㄴ, and 시 — 만듭니다, 만드세요, 만드니까 — but the ㄹ stays before vowel endings, giving the polite present 만들어요 (never 만드러요) and the suggestion 만들까요. A key contrast is 만들다 vs 하다: both can translate as 'make/do', but 만들다 implies producing a tangible result that did not exist before (케이크를 만들다 'make a cake'), whereas 하다 is to perform an activity (요리를 하다 'do cooking'). Also distinguish 짓다 ('to build/construct' houses, and to compose names/poems, 집을 짓다) from 만들다, which is the broad everyday 'make'. The English-speaker pitfall is mishandling the irregular in both directions: dropping the ㄹ before a vowel (만드러요) or keeping it before a consonant (만들습니다 instead of 만듭니다).

usage: the subject/skill learned takes the object marker 을/를
배우고 싶다 expresses the wish to learn
the source person takes 한테/에게서, not 에서
examples: 저는 한국어를 배워요.
I learn Korean.
two vowels contract: 배우 + 어요 → 배워요
요즘 친구한테 기타를 배우고 있어요.
These days I'm learning guitar from a friend.
source person takes 한테; 고 있다 = ongoing
저는 운전을 배워서 회사에 차로 가고 싶어요.
I want to learn to drive and go to work by car.
real goal-linked sentence; 배워서 connects reason to plan
nuance: 배우다 means 'to learn / acquire a skill or subject' and takes the object marker 을/를: 한국어를 배워요. It is a regular verb, but the stem ends in the vowel 우, so when 어요 attaches the two vowels contract into 워 — 배우 + 어요 → 배워요 (not 배우어요), past 배웠어요. The natural partner verb is 가르치다 ('to teach'), the giving side of the same act; and the person you learn from takes 한테/에게서 (사람) — 선생님한테 배워요 — never the place particle 에서 for the source. Contrast 배우다 with 공부하다 (工夫하다, 'to study'): 공부하다 is the effort of studying (sitting down, reviewing, hitting the books), while 배우다 is the result of acquiring a skill or being taught it, often from someone. So you 공부하다 for an exam at your desk but 배우다 the piano from a teacher. The English-speaker pitfall is writing the uncontracted 배우어요, and saying 학원에서 배우다 to mean 'learn from the academy' — 에서 marks where, while the human source must take 한테/에게서.

usage: the subject taught takes the object marker 을/를
가르쳐 + 주세요 asks someone to teach you as a favor
천천히 'slowly' is a polite softener in requests
examples: 선생님이 한국어를 가르쳐요.
The teacher teaches Korean.
치 + 어요 contracts to 쳐요
저는 학생들에게 영어를 가르쳐요.
I teach English to students.
double object pattern: 에게 = learner, 을 = subject
이 한자 좀 가르쳐 주세요. 발음을 모르겠어요.
Could you teach me this character? I don't know how it's read.
real request with a reason; 좀 softens it
nuance: 가르치다 means 'to teach / instruct' and is the giving counterpart of 배우다 ('to learn'). It is a regular verb whose stem ends in 치, so 치 + 어요 contracts to 쳐요 — the polite present is 가르쳐요, past 가르쳤어요. Its argument structure is the classic give-pattern: the learner (recipient) takes 에게 or casual 한테, and the subject taught takes 을/를 — 학생들에게 영어를 가르쳐요. Compare also with the honorific 가르침 ('teachings/guidance', a noun) and the polite request 가르쳐 주세요, which is how you say 'please show/tell me'. The English-speaker pitfall is mixing up 가르치다 with 가리키다, and forgetting that the person taught takes 에게/한테 (not 을/를), so 'teach the students' is 학생들에게 가르쳐요, with the lesson, not the student, as the 를-object.

usage: the person helped takes the object marker 을/를
key survival phrase — already polite, no extra 주세요 needed
좀 softens the request and sounds more natural
offering help; the 르 stem of 주다 keeps ㄹ before 까요
examples: 제가 도와줄게요.
I'll help you.
줄게요 = a friendly promise to help; spoken offer
친구가 저를 많이 도와줬어요.
My friend helped me a lot.
past 도와줬어요; the helper takes 이/가, helped person 를
짐이 무거운데 좀 도와주세요.
The luggage is heavy, so please help me.
real request: 는데 gives the reason, 좀 softens it

usage: with an object (transitive) the thing started takes 을/를
without a doer (intransitive) the thing takes 이/가
I start again / let's start over
examples: 수업이 아홉 시에 시작해요.
Class starts at nine.
time at 에; intransitive, so 수업이
저는 지난달에 새 일을 시작했어요.
I started a new job last month.
transitive past; 일을 시작했어요
준비됐어요? 그럼 이제 시작할까요?
Ready? Then shall we start now?
real suggestion before an activity
nuance: 시작하다 means 'to start / begin' and is a Sino-Korean 하다 verb — 시작 (始作, literally 始 'begin' + 作 'make/do', i.e. 'set in motion') plus 하다. As a 하다 verb it conjugates regularly with 하다 → 해요: 시작해요 / 시작합니다 / 시작했어요. A point that trips learners is that 시작하다 works both transitively and intransitively: with a doer it takes an object (저는 일을 시작해요 'I start work', 을/를), and with no doer the thing simply begins and takes the subject marker (수업이 시작해요 'class starts', 이/가). Contrast it with the pure intransitive 시작되다 (始作되다, 'to be started/begin'), which is more formal and never takes an object — 회의가 시작됐어요 'the meeting began'. Its natural opposite is 끝나다 ('to end'). The English-speaker pitfalls are (1) conjugating the 하다 wrongly as 시작하요 instead of 시작해요, and (2) forcing an object onto the no-doer case (수업을 시작해요 when you simply mean class begins) — when nothing actively starts it, use 수업이 시작해요 or the passive 시작돼요.

usage: intransitive: the thing that ends takes 이/가
다 'all/completely' is the natural partner of 끝나다
contrast: with an object use the transitive 끝내다, not 끝나다
examples: 수업이 세 시에 끝나요.
Class ends at three.
time at 에; intransitive 수업이
오늘 일이 일찍 끝났어요.
Work ended early today.
the event ends on its own, so 일이 (이/가)
이 일만 끝내면 집에 갈 수 있어요.
Once I finish just this task I can go home.
real plan: a doer finishes it, so the transitive 끝내다
nuance: 끝나다 means 'to end / be over / finish' as something that happens by itself — it is intransitive, so the thing that ends takes the subject marker 이/가: 수업이 끝나요, past 끝났어요 (끝나 + 았어요). The essential pairing is with its transitive twin 끝내다 ('to finish/end something'), used when a person actively brings an action to a close with an object: 저는 일을 끝내요 ('I finish the work', 을/를). This 끝나다 (happens) vs 끝내다 (someone does it) split mirrors 시작하다 family logic and is one of Korean's classic intransitive/transitive verb pairs (like 켜지다/켜다, 열리다/열다). The natural opposite is 시작하다 ('to begin'). A nuance of completion: 다 끝났어요 ('it's all done') is the everyday way to announce something is finished, and 끝 alone is an interjection meaning 'the end'. The English-speaker pitfall is using 끝나다 with an object — saying 일을 끝나요 by analogy to English 'I end the work' — when an actor finishes something it must be the transitive 일을 끝내요.

usage: the thing asked about takes the object marker 을/를
let me ask just one thing
물어보다 'ask and see' is the everyday spoken form
an honored person takes 께 (honorific of 에게)
물어봐도 돼요 politely requests permission to ask
examples: 저는 모르는 것을 선생님께 물어요.
I ask the teacher about things I don't know.
honorific recipient 께; thing asked 것을
모르면 저한테 물어보세요.
If you don't know, ask me.
casual recipient 한테; 물어보다 is warmer than plain 묻다
길을 몰라서 경찰관에게 물어봤어요.
I didn't know the way, so I asked a police officer.
past of 물어보다; 에게 marks the person asked
nuance: 묻다 means 'to ask (a question / inquire)' and takes the object marker 을/를 for the thing asked about: 길을 물어요. It is a ㄷ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the stem ㄷ changes to ㄹ, giving 물어요 and 물었어요 and 물을 거예요, but before consonant endings the ㄷ stays — 묻습니다, 묻고, 묻지 마세요. The person you ask takes 에게/한테, or honorific 께 for someone of higher status: 선생님께 물어요. In real speech Koreans far more often say 물어보다 ('ask and see', literally 묻다 + 보다), which sounds softer and more tentative than the bare, slightly abrupt 묻다 — so 물어보세요 ('please ask') is the natural request, not 물으세요. Two contrasts: do not confuse this 묻다 with the homograph 묻다 meaning 'to bury' (regular: 땅에 묻다), and distinguish 묻다 ('ask a question') from 부탁하다 ('to request a favor'). The English-speaker pitfall is keeping the ㄷ before a vowel to say 묻어요 (which actually reads as the 'bury' verb) instead of the irregular 물어요.
